metadata.title: Job Tasks and Wages in Developed Countries: Evidence from PIAAC

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC microdata for 19 developed countries and restricts the analytic sample to employee respondents aged 25–54 with hourly wages between 0 and 150 USD (PPP), excluding non-profit firms, agriculture, self-employed workers, and cases missing information needed for task construction. The authors report that regressions are conducted using complex sampling weights, with weights applied so that countries are weighted equally; this is used in the log-wage task price models (Tables 6 and A.4) and in the country-interaction models (Tables 7 and A.5). Standard errors are clustered at the occupation level, reflecting within-occupation correlation. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight inference is not extracted.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that observations with missing information on items used for task construction are excluded, but it does not provide a formal missing-data handling method for the remaining variables (e.g., whether any additional imputation was used). Plausible values are used for numeracy skills (the paper reports results for all 10 plausible values), but the missing-data strategy beyond task-item availability is not fully documented. This is a reporting gap for missingness beyond the explicit exclusion rule.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample includes PIAAC employee respondents aged 25–54 with hourly wages between 0 and 150 USD (PPP). The study excludes workers in non-profit firms and agriculture, excludes self-employed workers, and includes both full-time and part-time salaried workers. It further excludes workers for whom some information is missing on the items used for task construction. Task intensities are constructed from PIAAC questionnaire items using a PCA-based approach (first component) and the task price regressions are estimated using complex sampling weights (countries weighted equally) and conducted for all plausible values of numeracy skills.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — task prices for abstract tasks
main_findings.target_variable: Abstract task price (within-occupation wage premium, log hourly earnings)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Log-wage regression (Table 6, AH + Numeracy Skills): Abstract (individual) coefficient = 0.0241 (SE 0.00669), significant; Abstract (occupation level) coefficient = 0.122 (SE 0.0186), significant. Conclusion in text: within occupations, +1 SD abstract tasks associated with +3.3 log-point wage premium.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC worker-level data for 19 developed countries, the study leveraged abstract task endowment together with numeracy skills and key demographic/job covariates to estimate abstract task prices in log hourly earnings, finding that higher abstract task intensity is associated with a positive within-occupation wage premium (about +3.3 log points per SD). This indicates that labor-market demand for non-routine cognitive work is strongly rewarded, supporting policies that expand adult numeracy and advanced problem-solving skills to help workers access higher-paying task bundles, while noting the paper does not provide causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — task prices for routine tasks
main_findings.target_variable: Routine task price (within-occupation wage decrease, log hourly earnings)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Log-wage regression (Table 6, AH + Numeracy Skills): Routine (individual) coefficient = -0.0227 (SE 0.0063), significant; Routine (occupation level) coefficient = -0.00008 (SE 0.0146), not significant. Conclusion in text: within occupations, routine tasks associated with -2.6 log-point wage decrease per SD.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC worker-level data for 19 developed countries, the study leveraged routine task endowment together with numeracy skills and demographic/job covariates to estimate routine task prices in log hourly earnings, finding that higher routine task intensity is associated with a negative within-occupation wage effect (about -2.6 log points per SD). This indicates that automation-linked routinization pressures may reduce earnings for workers performing routine tasks, implying that reskilling and job redesign toward non-routine activities could mitigate wage losses, though causality cannot be inferred from the observational design.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — task prices for manual tasks
main_findings.target_variable: Manual task price (within-occupation wage decrease, log hourly earnings)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Log-wage regression (Table 6, AH + Numeracy Skills): Manual (individual) coefficient = -0.0382 (SE 0.0052), significant; Manual (occupation level) coefficient = -0.0229 (SE 0.0094), significant. Conclusion in text: within occupations, manual tasks associated with -2.9 log-point wage decrease per SD.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC worker-level data for 19 developed countries, the study leveraged manual task endowment together with numeracy skills and demographic/job covariates to estimate manual task prices in log hourly earnings, finding that higher manual task intensity is associated with a negative within-occupation wage effect (about -2.9 log points per SD). This indicates that earnings penalties are concentrated in task bundles involving manual work, suggesting that wage-protection and training policies should target transitions away from manual-intensive roles, while recognizing the estimates are conditional correlations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (2012/2015 waves; developed countries; worker-level wages) — cross-country heterogeneity in task prices
main_findings.target_variable: Country-differential task prices (interaction effects with development and institutions)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-interaction model (Table 7): Abstract tasks—Average Return = 0.019 (SE not shown in excerpt) in column (10); interactions reported as significant in text: union coverage and EPL have significant negative interactions with abstract task prices; for routine and manual tasks, interactions with GDP and ICT capital stock are positive. Additional text-based simulation ranges: ICT capital stock per worker implies abstract task prices from -0.08 (Chile) to 0.05 (Norway); EPL conditional abstract task prices from -0.01 (Belgium) to 0.06 (US).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC worker-level data for 19 developed countries, the study leveraged task endowment measures and country-level development/institution variables (GDP per capita, ICT capital stock, union coverage, and employment protection legislation) to model cross-country differences in task prices, finding that labor-market institutions and development conditions systematically attenuate or amplify task-related wage premiums/penalties. This indicates that policy levers such as union coverage and employment protection legislation may shape how technological change translates into wage inequality across task types, though the paper explicitly avoids causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This paper uses PIAAC worker-level data for 19 developed countries to construct three job-task intensity measures (abstract, routine, manual) from questionnaire items and to estimate “task prices” in log hourly wages. The analytic sample comprises 37,607 employees aged 25–54 with wages between 0 and 150 USD (PPP), excluding non-profit firms, agriculture, self-employment, and cases missing task-item information. The study reports that within occupations, a one-standard-deviation increase in abstract tasks is associated with a 3.3-log-point wage premium, while routine and manual tasks are associated with 2.6- and 2.9-log-point wage decreases, respectively. Cross-country heterogeneity is explored via interactions with development and labor-market institutions; union coverage and employment protection legislation show significant relationships with abstract-task prices, and development/ICT conditions interact with routine and manual task prices. The paper uses complex sampling weights (countries weighted equally) and runs regressions across all plausible values for numeracy skills, but it does not apply machine learning algorithms; therefore, the findings are correlational rather than predictive/causal.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an econometric analysis of task measurement and wage regressions rather than a machine-learning prediction/classification study. As a result, no ML algorithms are evaluated (ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty) and the primary ML model is not applicable. The extraction therefore focuses on the empirical regression-based task-price outcomes and their policy interpretation.
